text: Few passages in the Bible have had a stranger interpretive history than the account of the *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") in Genesis 6. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and still read as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, elaborated a tradition of fallen angels, the Watchers, who descended to corrupt humanity by two means: forbidden teaching and miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this reading. Augustine would have none of it. In *City of God* he rejected the angelic interpretation and favored a Sethite genealogy, in which the sons of God are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men are the line of Cain. Other readers have looked eastward, setting the passage beside ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The chapter also introduces the flood narrative, and that narrative belongs to a broader Mesopotamian tradition. Its fullest surviving forms are the *Atrahasis* epic and tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (the Utnapishtim narrative), both of which contain close parallels to the biblical story. The vocabulary is odd as well. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds, *tevah* ("ark," "chest"), is used elsewhere in Scripture only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.
